sections.title: Section 1
sections.context: A customer phones a furniture store to arrange the delivery of a wardrobe

transcript.text: Good afternoon, Hartwell Furniture, deliveries desk, Chloe speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I bought a wardrobe in your Milton Road branch on Saturday, and the assistant said I should ring this number to sort out the delivery.
That's right, I can do that now. Can I start with your name, please?
It's Laura Deighton.
Deighton... is that D-A-Y-T-O-N?
No, everyone writes it that way, but it's the old spelling — D-E-I-G-H-T-O-N.
D-E-I-G-H-T-O-N. Lovely. And a mobile number, in case the driver needs to reach you?

It's oh-seven-nine-one-three, double four, six... five, oh, nine. Hmm — no, hang on, sorry, I've given you the ending of my work phone. Mine finishes five-two-nine, not five-oh-nine. So oh-seven-nine-one-three, four-four-six, five-two-nine.
Zero seven nine one three, four four six, five two nine. Got it. And the delivery address?
It's Flat 2, number 27, Wyndham Close. Shall I spell the street? W-Y-N-D-H-A-M.
W-Y-N-D-H-A-M, Wyndham Close. Thank you. Now, the order itself — I can see two wardrobes on the Saturday list. Was yours the pine one?
No — I did look hard at the pine, but in the end I chose the oak one. It was the last display model, apparently.
The oak wardrobe, yes, here it is. Right, deliveries to your postcode go out on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Which suits you?
Thursday, please — ideally the morning, before I do the school run at lunchtime.
Let me look... I'm sorry, Thursday morning is completely full this week. I can offer you the Thursday afternoon instead, or the following Tuesday morning.
Oh. No, I don't want to wait another week — the afternoon will have to do. Thursday afternoon, then.
Thursday afternoon it is. Now, two optional extras. We have an assembly service — the drivers will build the wardrobe in the room you choose. That's forty pounds.
Forty? Mmm, it's tempting, but no — my brother's a joiner, he'll put it together for nothing. I'll skip that.
No problem. The other one is removal: for fifteen pounds the crew will take away your old wardrobe and recycle it.
Oh, now that I do want. The old wardrobe is enormous and I've no way of shifting it. Yes, add the removal, please.
Done — so that's the delivery plus fifteen pounds. Now, is there anything the driver should know about access?
Yes, quite a lot, actually. Wyndham Close itself is a dead end and there's never anywhere to stop. Drivers usually park round the corner in Bell Lane and carry things through the passage.
Park in Bell Lane, use the passage — I'll put that on the sheet. You said Flat 2. Is that ground floor?
First floor, and there's no lift, just the staircase. It's wide enough, but I keep plant pots on the steps — I'll move those before they come, otherwise there's no room to turn.
Please do — the crew can't lift over anything left on the stairs. Last thing: on the Thursday morning you'll get a text message giving you a two-hour window, so you're not waiting in all afternoon.
A text on the day — perfect. Thanks so much for your help, Chloe.
You're welcome, Ms Deighton. We'll see you Thursday.

sections.title: Section 2
sections.context: A project officer describes the restoration of a coastal footpath

transcript.text: Good morning, and welcome to the open day for the Saltmere Coast Path project. I'm Megan Ellis, the project officer, and I'll quickly explain what we're doing, where everything is, and how you can get involved.

First, some history. Parts of the path between the car park and the harbour have been closed for nearly two years. People often assume it was worn out by the sheer number of walkers, and some locals blame the farm vehicles that used to cross it. In fact neither did the real harm: it was two winters of severe storms that tore out whole sections of the surface and brought the cliff edge back several metres.

Now, the money. The council has put in a share, and local businesses have donated timber and stone. But the great bulk of the funding — about four-fifths of it — comes from a National Lottery grant awarded last spring. Without that, none of this would be happening.

Before designing anything we ran a public consultation, and the results surprised us. A few people asked for better signs, and some wanted more litter bins. But by far the most common request — over half the forms we received — was for more seating, especially from older walkers with nowhere to rest on the whole three-mile stretch. So there will be twelve new benches along the route.

Right, the plan you've been given. You're standing at the car park at the southern end, and the path runs north along the coast, finishing at the harbour. The first thing you'll see, immediately next to the car park, is the new welcome shelter, where the route maps are displayed.

Follow the path north and you cross the wooden footbridge over the creek. Just beyond the footbridge, on the seaward side, we've rebuilt the bird hide, looking out over the mudflats — at low tide you'll see hundreds of waders from there.

Further on, the path climbs to the headland, the highest point of the route. We had originally planned to rebuild the viewing platform up there, where the old one stood, but surveys showed the cliff edge has retreated too far, so the platform has been moved: it now sits on the landward side of the path, set back from the cliff, just before you reach the headland. The view is almost as good — and it will still be there in thirty years.
At the far end, near the harbour, behind the old lifeboat station, we've set up the tool store, where our volunteers sign in and collect equipment.

One disappointment. The flight of steps down to the beach at Craven Point was due to reopen this August, but our contractor found the rock face behind them is unstable, and that work can't be done while seabirds are nesting. So the steps will stay closed until the spring. Please don't climb the barriers — the drop is severe.

Finally, volunteering. Work parties run every Wednesday and Saturday. All tools and gloves are provided — but you must bring your own boots, sturdy ones, because the ground is rough and often wet. And if you can't dig, you can still help: we post a progress report every week on the project blog, and sharing it genuinely helps our next funding application. Now — any questions?

sections.title: Section 3
sections.context: Two students plan an episode of their linguistics society podcast

transcript.text: Right, Josh — episode four. We promised the committee a plan by tonight, so let's pin things down. Are we still doing language change?

That's what we pitched, but I've been sketching an outline and honestly, it's hopeless. Language change is a whole lecture course — sound shifts, grammar, borrowing, slang... We'd end up skating over everything and saying nothing.
I had exactly the same feeling. So what if we take just one thread? Everyone asks me about new words — you know, how something like 'rizz' ends up in the dictionary.
Yes! That's the episode: how a new word gets into the dictionary. Who decides, what evidence they need, how long it takes. It's concrete, and it's got a story shape.
Which brings us to the guest. You suggested Professor Halloran. I emailed him, and to be fair, he replied within the hour and said he'd happily do it.
But...?

But I went and listened to the keynote he gave last term. Josh, honestly — ten minutes on corpus lemmatisation. He's brilliant, but for a general audience it would be completely impenetrable. I don't think we can use him.
Hmm. I hate turning down someone who's willing... but you're right, the podcast is for freshers and the public, not specialists. So who instead?
Kate Munro. She's an editor at a dictionary publisher — she literally sits on the panel that approves new entries, and I've heard her on the radio: she's funny, and she explains with examples.
Perfect. I'll email her today and offer her a choice of dates. Now — where do we record? I assumed the media suite, same as episode three.
Can't — the media suite is reserved for exam recordings all this month. The technician suggested the library: there's a small recording booth on the top floor you can book by the hour.
A booth? Will three people even fit?
It seats four, apparently, and the microphones are already set up. I'll book the booth for the week after next.
Fine. Now, the opening. I still think we start with a comedy sketch — you and me acting out a caveman inventing a word. It'd be memorable.

Memorable, yes, but for the wrong reasons — we're not actors, Josh. What if we open with a real clip instead? I could take the recorder into town on Saturday and ask passers-by what new words they've noticed. Thirty seconds of real voices, then we come in.
Street interviews... actually, that's better than the sketch, isn't it? Real people, real data. Okay, you've convinced me. You do the vox pops, and I'll write the link that follows them.
Deal. Length — the committee said episodes can now run to thirty minutes... no, wait, sorry, I'm thinking of last year's rule. They cut it this term: twenty-five minutes maximum, including credits.
Twenty-five. Tight, but doable if the interview is fifteen. And editing? The society wants everything uploaded on the Monday.
Which means the rough edit has to be finished by Friday, so we've got the weekend for fixes. Your turn to edit — I did the last three.
Fair enough, I'll edit. One more thing — every episode now needs a transcript on the website, for accessibility. That's new.
I'll do the transcript while you edit. Right — that's actually a plan.

sections.title: Section 4
sections.context: A lecture on animal navigation, focusing on sea turtles

transcript.text: Today: what may be the most remarkable navigator of all, the sea turtle. A loggerhead hatched in Florida will swim a circuit of the entire North Atlantic — some fifteen thousand kilometres, over a decade — and then return, as an adult, to breed on the very stretch of coast where she hatched.

How? Turtles carry a magnetic sense. The Earth's field varies predictably from place to place, and experiments show turtles detect two features of it: the field's strength, or intensity, and also its angle — the steepness at which the field lines meet the surface, which scientists call inclination. Together, the two values work rather like latitude and longitude, giving the animal what researchers call a magnetic map.

That map is stamped in early. Returning to breed at one's own birth beach is a behaviour biologists call natal homing, and the leading explanation is that hatchlings imprint on the magnetic signature of their birth beach in their first hours, then seek it out decades later. To be honest about the limits: the receptor has never been found, and the imprinting account is not yet fully proven.

The evidence is striking. In the classic experiments, hatchlings swam in water tanks surrounded by magnetic coils, which reproduce the field of any point on the globe — and they headed in the direction that, at the simulated location, would have kept them inside the warm Atlantic currents. The precision in the wild is astonishing: genetic studies show most adult females nest within a few kilometres of their own hatching site.

Now to correct a popular story, because it matters for conservation. Ask how a hatchling, emerging at night, finds the sea, and most people say it follows the moon. It is wrong: hatchlings tested under moonless, overcast skies find the water perfectly well. What they actually do is crawl towards the brightest horizon. For millions of years that was reliable, because the sea reflects starlight while the dunes stand dark behind the beach.

You can see what breaks that ancient rule: street lighting. On a developed coast the brightest horizon is no longer the sea but the road behind the beach, so instead of scrambling down to the water, hatchlings head inland, towards hotels and car parks. Many are taken by predators, and most of the rest die of exhaustion before dawn. In Florida alone, disorientation is estimated to kill hundreds of thousands of hatchlings a year.

The fix, encouragingly, is cheap and proven. Turtles are far less sensitive to long wavelengths, so towns that replace white lamps with red lights — shielded and mounted low — see disorientation fall dramatically, in some counties by more than three-quarters. No new technology is needed, just planning rules.

A subtler threat brings us back to the magnetic map. A beach's magnetic signature can be altered by human structures, and researchers now worry about the steel used in sea walls and other coastal defences, which measurably distorts the local field. If a returning female cannot recognise her natal beach, she may waste precious weeks searching. I stress the qualifier: so far this is demonstrated mainly in the laboratory. But an animal that reads the world through senses we lack can be harmed by changes we cannot even perceive. Next week: how salmon manage a comparable feat.

questions.explain: 'The field's strength, or intensity, and also its angle... which scientists call inclination' — the two values form the magnetic map.

questions.explain: The term is defined explicitly: 'a behaviour biologists call natal homing.'

questions.explain: 'Genetic studies show most adult females nest within a few kilometres of their own hatching site.'

questions.prompt: Popular belief: hatchlings find the sea by following the ______.
questions.explain: The lecturer raises the popular explanation in order to correct it — hatchlings find water even under moonless, overcast skies.

questions.explain: 'What they actually do is crawl towards the brightest horizon' — historically the sea, which reflects starlight.

questions.explain: Cause and effect: on developed coasts the brightest horizon is the road, 'so instead of scrambling down to the water, hatchlings head inland'.

questions.prompt: The steel used in ______ may distort a beach's magnetic signature.
questions.explain: 'The steel used in sea walls and other coastal defences... measurably distorts the local field' — though the lecturer stresses this is so far shown mainly in the laboratory.
